'''Bo Yngve Thidé''' (born 8 January 1948) is a Swedish [[physicist]] and [[professor emeritus]] at [[Uppsala University]]. He has studied radio waves and other electromagnetic radiation in space, particularly their interaction with matter and fields.

Thidé was born in [[Gothenburg]], Sweden.{{citation needed|date=August 2022}} He received his B.Sc. in 1972,<ref>{{Cite news |date=8 May 1972 |title=akademiska examina |pages=2 |work=[[Svenska Dagbladet]] |language=sv}}</ref> his M.Sc. in 1973,<ref>{{Cite news |date=16 July 1973 |title=Akademiska examina |pages=12 |work=[[Svenska Dagbladet]] |language=sv}}</ref> and defended his Ph.D. thesis on semiclassical quantum theory at [[Uppsala University]] in 1979. His Ph.D. was obtained under the supervision of professor [[Per Olof Fröman]] at the Department of Theoretical Physics, Uppsala University. He has worked at the Swedish Institute of Space Physics in Uppsala<ref name="techworld">{{cite news |last1=Städje |first1=Jörgen |title=Tumlande radiovågor ändrar bilden av universum |url=https://techworld.idg.se/2.2524/1.337064/tumlande-radiovagor-andrar-bilden-av-universum |access-date=27 July 2022 |work=TechWorld |issue=8/2010 |date=16 September 2010 |pages=70–72 |language=Swedish}}</ref> since 1980, where he has been a professor since 2000.

In 1981, Bo Thidé discovered electromagnetic emissions stimulated by powerful [[radio waves]] in the [[ionosphere]] during experiments in August 1981 at the [[EISCAT]] facility in [[Tromsø]], Norway.<ref>{{cite journal|author1=B. Thidé |author2=H. Kopka |author3=P. Stubbe |name-list-style=amp | title=Observations of Stimulated Scattering of a Strong High-Frequency Radio Wave in the Ionosphere| journal=Physical Review Letters| year=1982| volume=49| issue=21| pages=1561–1564| doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.49.1561| bibcode=1982PhRvL..49.1561T}}</ref> For the first time it was shown that the plasma turbulence excited by powerful radio waves in the ionosphere radiates secondary electromagnetic radiation that can be detected and analysed on the ground. These stimulated electromagnetic emissions (SEE) exhibit a rich spectral structure, particularly near harmonics of the ionospheric electron gyro frequency. The SEE technique is now a useful tool in plasma turbulence research. For his discovery, Thidé was awarded the Edlund Prize of the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences in 1991.

In the mid-1980s, Thidé published a series of papers together with Bengt Lundborg on a highly accurate analytic approximation method to calculate the full three-dimensional wave pattern, [[spin angular momentum of light|spin angular momentum]] ([[Polarization (waves)|polarization]]) and other properties of radio waves propagating in an inhomogeneous, magnetized, collisional [[plasma (physics)|plasma]].

Thidé was involved in a project in [[The Netherlands]] where 12&nbsp;500 antenna designed to analyse [[solar storm]]s were built.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Westman |first=Henrik |date=16 October 2004 |title=Små klot håller koll på rymden |pages=9 |work=[[Dagens Industri]] |language=sv}}</ref> In 2001 he led the LOIS-project, that placed tens of thousands of antenna in southern Sweden. The project was a subsidiary of the multinational [[Low-Frequency Array (LOFAR)|LOFAR project]] headed by The Netherlands and aimed to find traces of the first hydrogen atom formed during [[Big Bang]].<ref>{{Cite news |last=Peruzzi |first=Britt |date=21 October 2001 |title=Växsjö kan lösa universums gåta |pages=12 |work=[[Aftonbladet]] |language=sv}}</ref>

Together with colleagues from Italy and Spain, Thidé discovered in 2010 a new phenomenon in [[General Relativity]] which allows the detection of [[spinning black hole]]s by analysing the [[Orbital angular momentum of light|orbital angular momentum]] and [[optical vortex]] structure of radiation from the [[accretion disk]] near the black holes. The results were published in [[Nature Physics]].<ref>{{cite journal|author1=F. Tamburini |author2=B. Thidé |author3=G. Molina-Terriza |author4=G. Anzolin |title=Twisting light around rotating black holes|journal=Nature Physics| year=2011| volume=7| issue=3| pages=195–197| doi=10.1038/NPHYS1907|bibcode = 2011NatPh...7..195T |arxiv = 1104.3099 |s2cid=28065268 }}</ref> He was later part of a team which discovered that radio beams from fast-spinning black holes are twisted.<ref name="bt2020">{{cite news |last1=Andersson |first1=Felicia |title=Rymdforskare kastar nytt ljus över svarta hål |work=[[Borlänge Tidning]] |date=21 May 2020 |page=5 |language=Swedish}}</ref>

Thidé has advocated [[Orbital angular momentum multiplexing]] for radio transmissions, opening up additional degrees of freedom.<ref>Fabrizio Tamburini, Elettra Mari, Anna Sponselli, Bo Thidé, Antonio Bianchini and Filippo Romanato (2012) "Encoding many channels on the same frequency through radio vorticity: first experimental test" ''New J. Phys.'' '''14''' 033001 [https://dx.doi.org/10.1088/1367-2630/14/3/033001 doi:10.1088/1367-2630/14/3/033001]</ref> Thidé is the author of the book ''Electromagnetic Field Theory'', which is used in the course Classical Electrodynamics at [[Uppsala University]] and [[University of Padua]]. He has also worked on fiber optics technology.<ref name="svt2015">{{cite news |last1=Dahlberg |first1=Markus |title=Rymdforskare tar fram ny bredbandsteknik |url=https://www.svt.se/nyheter/lokalt/gavleborg/rymdforskare-tar-fram-ny-bredbandsteknik |access-date=27 July 2022 |work=[[Sveriges Television]] |date=5 May 2015 |language=Swedish}}</ref><ref name="ht2015">{{cite news |last1=Tomassen |first1=Emil |title=Framtidens fiber forskas fram av Bo |work=[[Hudiksvalls Tidning]] |page=7 |language=Swedish}}</ref>

Since 2016, he lives outside [[Söderhamn]], where he continues his research from home.<ref name="bt2020" />
